full_judgment:
5. Mr. Ahmed Nowshed Jamil, the teamed Advocate appearing for the petitioner submits that the appellate Court below on serious misconception of law came to a wrong conclusion that a Hindu widow governed by Dayavaga School of law did not inherit agricultural land from her husband. He referring the Hindu Women's Rights to Property Act, 1937 (in short, the Act) submits that sub-section (1) of section 3 of the Act clearly provides that when a Hindu husband govemeded by Dayavaga School of Hindu Law died intestate leaving any property his widow or widows shall be entitled in respect of such property to the same share as one son. He categorically submits that the Act provides no scope to discriminate among the property left by a Hindu husband like agricultural or non-agricultural land etcetera. 

 "When a Hindu governed by the Dayabhag School of Hindu Law dies intestate leaving any property, and when a Hindu governed by any other school of Hindu Law or by customary law dies intestate leaving separate property, his widow, or if there is more than one widow all his widows together, shall, subject to the provisions of sub-section (3), be entitled in respect of property in respect of which he dies intestate to the same share as a son" 

 "Considering the aforesaid provisions of sub-sections (1) and (3) of section 3 of the Hindu Women's Rights to the Property Act (XVIII of 1937) it clearly appears that during the period of her life time a Hindu widow is a complete owner and co-sharer of any property or holding in question with the right to claim partition and consequently having the right to claim pre-emption under section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act." (Para 3 of the judgment)
